title: Throughput tuning technical deep dive - BrightScale
summary: SE-led deep dive on throughput tuning for BrightScale's LLM workloads. Covered continuous batching behavior, scheduler settings (max_num_seqs, batch timeout), token limits, KV cache warmup patterns, quantization tradeoffs, and VPC deployment constraints. Agreed to run a targeted benchmark and share a tuned config and benchmark sheet.

transcript:
Meeting header:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Alex from Redwood here, we got Priya our SE, Jordan on SRE notes. BrightScale team, thanks for the time.
[00:10] Maya Jensen: Hi Alex, hi Priya, thanks. Maya here. We're excited to dig in on throughput. Quick context: we run a mix of chat + summarization, tail latencies are what kill us right now.
[00:24] Priya Nair: Great, can you outline your P50/P95 targets and current hardware?
[00:30] Maya Jensen: Target is P95 <= 450ms for short chat (<=128 tokens). Currently we're on a self-hosted cluster of A100-ish instances and seeing P95 around 1.1s during bursts.
[00:42] Tom Alvarez: Also request patterns are spiky, a lot of small sequences, many concurrent users.
[00:50] Priya Nair: Okay that fits the continuous-batching problem. We'll walk through scheduler knobs, max_num_seqs, and token limits.
[01:00] Jordan Lee: Quick note, during our initial perf run we saw KV-cache warmup adding ~60-100ms for first request after idle.
[01:12] Maya Jensen: That KV cache behavior is a big one for us, we can't pre-warm everything.
[01:18] Priya Nair: Right. So first slide – continuous batching: Redwood runtime keeps accepting requests into a native batch until either batch size hits max_num_seqs or batch timeout fires. The tradeoff is latency vs throughput. If you set max_num_seqs high and timeout long, you get better GPU utilization but higher tail latency.
[01:38] Tom Alvarez: What are typical starting points? We tried default max_num_seqs=32 and saw queuing lag.
[01:45] Priya Nair: For A100 and chat-style short sequences, we often recommend starting with max_num_seqs=8 or 16 and batch_timeout 8-12ms, then increase if you need throughput. Also enable dynamic token packing if payloads vary.
[02:00] Maya Jensen: Can you explain dynamic token packing?
[02:05] Priya Nair: Sure — it packs multiple short sequences into the same CUDA batch to maximize tokens per forward. It's different to naive seq-based batching. It reduces wasted compute on padding. There are knobs to prefer latency (pack less) or throughput (pack aggressively).
[02:20] Alex Chen: Also watch out for max_total_tokens per batch. If you only control max_num_seqs but not tokens, you can still overflow and force smaller effective batches.
[02:30] Ravi Gupta: How does KV cache interact with batching? We noticed cold-cache requests slower but subsequent recency helps.
[02:38] Priya Nair: KV cache is per-model and per-sequence; when we pack sequences, the runtime keeps KV caches in GPU memory. The warmup cost is mostly first-token decoding and initial KV load; after that, repeated calls benefit. For spiky traffic we recommend a small fraction of reserved warmup slots or keep-alive to reduce thrash.
[02:56] Tom Alvarez: Is that the 'keeper' process we saw in the doc?
[03:00] Priya Nair: Yes, the keeper maintains active KV caches for hot sessions. You can set keeper_size and keeper_ttl. Increasing keeper_size reduces cold starts but increases GPU memory footprint.
[03:12] Maya Jensen: Memory is tight — we can't afford large keeper_size across many models.
[03:18] Priya Nair: Then consider selective keeper policies: pin only high-frequency user sessions or conversations over a threshold. Also consider offloading older KV segments to host memory if you have bandwidth.
[03:30] Alex Chen: Next, scheduler knobs — there's a priority-based scheduler that can do latency-first queues. If you tag a route as latency-sensitive, it will cap batch sizes and fallback quickly. Useful for your chat route versus long-form summarize jobs.
[03:45] Tom Alvarez: Are those tags in the route config? And can we test them without deploying Dedicated?
[03:50] Priya Nair: Yes, route-level config. You can test it on Hosted or a small Dedicated pool. We can push a testing policy in your sandbox.
[03:57] [04:00] Speaker 1: (murmur)
[04:02] Maya Jensen: Token limits question — we see some requests with long context lengths triggering the model to slow. How do you recommend capping tokens?
[04:10] Priya Nair: Set a route-level max_input_tokens and max_total_tokens. Also enable early rejection thresholds and provide client-side warnings. On the server side, you can enforce token trimming strategies (priority-keep recent vs keep first).
[04:25] Ravi Gupta: If we trim, we need deterministic behavior so app logic knows which context was used.
[04:31] Alex Chen: We log the final prompt lengths and provide audit tokens. That ties into observability in Console.
[04:38] Tom Alvarez: Quantization — we saw a 2.2x throughput gain with int8 but some quality diff. Thoughts?
[04:46] Priya Nair: Quantization is model dependent. int8 or q4_0 can give big perf wins but watch for hallucination or softened logits. We recommend per-workload evals: run your eval prompts across quantized variants and compare metric deltas. Redwood Optimize can suggest quant profiles.
[05:03] Maya Jensen: Can we do a mixed profile? Critical flows on float16, batch jobs on int8?
[05:10] Priya Nair: Yes — runtime supports model variants and can fallback. You can route critical endpoints to higher-precision variants. That's common enterprise pattern.
[05:20] Jordan Lee: We did an internal micro-benchmark: mixed-profile routing added ~5% overhead but saved 30-40% on GPU cost.
[05:28] Tom Alvarez: About VPC/on-prem — if we go private, how different are the knobs? Will Keeper/Batching still work same as Hosted?
[05:36] Priya Nair: The runtime is identical. Private installs include the same scheduler and keeper components. Differences are in networking, KMS integration, and you'll control autoscaler. We provide ops runbook for tuning.
[05:48] Lina Gomez: Security: do you support HSM-backed KMS and customer-managed keys?
[05:52] Alex Chen: Yes, we integrate with common KMS/HSM providers. We'll share security-pack.pdf and SOC2 controls.
[05:58] Maya Jensen: Can you walk through an example tuning plan?
[06:02] Priya Nair: Sure. Step one: baseline benchmark with your trace at current defaults to capture tail latency. Step two: run continuous-batching sweep: max_num_seqs=[4,8,16], batch_timeout=[4ms,8ms,12ms], token packing on/off. Capture P50/P95/P99 and GPU utilization. Step three: KV keeper tuning — keeper_size small, keeper_ttl tuned to session lengths. Step four: evaluate quantization variants with eval set. Step five: decide routing (latency vs throughput) and pin route configs. We'll produce a parameter file you can apply directly.
[06:36] Tom Alvarez: For the sweep, how long per config we should run? Minutes, hours?
[06:40] Priya Nair: For stable workloads, 5-10 minutes per setting can show trends, but for noisy production traces run 30-60 minutes. We'll pick a 30-minute run for your main configs.
[06:50] Maya Jensen: About monitoring — what dashboards do we get?
[06:54] Alex Chen: Console exposes token-level cost, per-route P95, batch sizes, queue length, KV hit rates, and memory usage. We can add custom traces for your golden prompts.
[07:06] Ravi Gupta: Do you expose per-sequence KV hit rate?
[07:08] Priya Nair: Yes, there's a KV_hit metric and keeper_evictions gauge.
[07:12] [07:20] Speaker 2: (background)
[07:22] Maya Jensen: One more — max_num_seqs interplay with CUDA kernels and fused attention, any gotchas?
[07:28] Priya Nair: Good point. For fused attention kernels, you see best perf when batch token counts align to warp sizes. There's some non-linearity: beyond certain batch token counts latency rises steeply. Our kernel selector picks best kernel variant based on batch token distribution; but you should avoid pathological distributions, e.g., many sequences with widely varying lengths that cause padding bloat.
[07:52] Tom Alvarez: Is there an auto-tuner?
[07:55] Priya Nair: We have an internal suggestion engine that recommends max_num_seqs and quantization per model/profile. Redwood Optimize will generate a config, but SE tuning is still recommended for sensitive apps.
[08:06] Maya Jensen: For our initial runs, can you provide a starter config?
[08:09] Alex Chen: Yes, Priya will drop a config and a bench spreadsheet link. We'll annotate recommended default + conservative settings.
[08:18] Tom Alvarez: Any notes about cold starts and autoscaler interactions? We saw cold autoscale adds 5-7s for new nodes.
[08:26] Priya Nair: Autoscaler warm pools and burst capacity help. For Dedicated you can reserve a small standby pool to avoid node spin-up. Also prefer model shards pinned to nodes if you have predictable load.
[08:38] Maya Jensen: Could we do all chat traffic on Dedicated and batch summarization on Hosted to save cost?
[08:44] Alex Chen: That's a common hybrid pattern. Use routing policies to send latency sensitive requests to Dedicated and best-effort to Hosted.
[08:51] Ravi Gupta: Regarding logs — we need audit logs retained for 12 months. Does Console support that?
[08:56] Alex Chen: Yes, retention is an add-on. We'll include details in the security pack.
[09:02] [09:10] Priya Nair: Let's go through a quick example config snippet: max_num_seqs: 8, batch_timeout_ms: 8, max_total_tokens: 4096, token_packing: aggressive, keeper_size: 250, keeper_ttl_sec: 300, route_priority: latency.
[09:28] Tom Alvarez: That sounds reasonable to try.
[09:31] Maya Jensen: Ok, let's plan the benchmark, I will get the traces to you.
[09:35] Alex Chen: Great. We'll run the sweep and share results. Any other questions?
[09:40] Lina Gomez: One small question on encryption in transit for Private — do you support mTLS for intra-node comms?
[09:46] Alex Chen: Yes, mTLS is supported for private deployments and we can show the manifest.
[09:50] Tom Alvarez: For the bench data, can you provide a template spreadsheet so we can compare?
[09:54] Priya Nair: Yes, we'll attach throughput-benchmarks.xlsx.
[09:58] Alex Chen: Alright we're at time, quick recap — list of next steps: Redwood provide tuned config + bench sheet (Priya), BrightScale provide traces and sample prompts (Tom), security docs exchange (Alex/Lina), follow-up scheduling.
[10:12] Maya Jensen: Thanks everyone. This was helpful.
[10:16] Alex Chen: Thanks, talk soon.
[10:20] END TRANSCRIPT

Notes: Transcription includes occasional mis-heard words and shorthand; proper nouns sometimes off. Links referenced: throughput-benchmarks.xlsx (placeholder link), security-pack.pdf (placeholder link).
